<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1280 720" width="1280" height="720">
  <!-- Background -->
  <rect x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="720" fill="#FFFFFF"/>
  <rect x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="6" fill="#1565C0"/>

  <!-- Page title -->
  <text x="60" y="58" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="28" font-weight="bold" fill="#212121">Key Takeaways: Design Principles for Efficient Multimodal Models</text>

  <!-- Takeaway box -->
  <rect x="60" y="74" width="1160" height="40" rx="6" fill="#1565C0" fill-opacity="0.06"/>
  <text x="80" y="100" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#1565C0">Five actionable design principles from SmolVLM — architectural efficiency matters more than raw scale.</text>

  <defs>
    <filter id="shadow9" x="-5%" y="-5%" width="115%" height="125%">
      <feGaussianBlur in="SourceAlpha" stdDeviation="6"/>
      <feOffset dx="0" dy="3" result="offsetBlur"/>
      <feFlood flood-color="#000000" flood-opacity="0.08" result="shadowColor"/>
      <feComposite in="shadowColor" in2="offsetBlur" operator="in" result="shadow"/>
      <feMerge>
        <feMergeNode in="shadow"/>
        <feMergeNode in="SourceGraphic"/>
      </feMerge>
    </filter>
  </defs>

  <!-- Takeaway 1 -->
  <rect x="60" y="130" width="1160" height="88" rx="10" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="#E0E0E0" stroke-width="1" filter="url(#shadow9)"/>
  <rect x="60" y="130" width="6" height="88" rx="3" fill="#1565C0"/>
  <rect x="80" y="144" width="44" height="44" rx="22" fill="#1565C0" fill-opacity="0.1"/>
  <text x="102" y="174" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="20" font-weight="bold" fill="#1565C0" text-anchor="middle">1</text>
  <text x="144" y="168" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="17" font-weight="bold" fill="#212121">Balance Encoder-LM Compute Allocation</text>
  <text x="144" y="194" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#616161">A 93M SigLIP-B/16 outperforms the 428M SigLIP-SO400M for the smallest LMs. Match encoder</text>
  <text x="144" y="212" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#616161">capacity to LM capacity — don't over-invest in vision when the language model is the bottleneck.</text>

  <!-- Takeaway 2 -->
  <rect x="60" y="232" width="1160" height="88" rx="10" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="#E0E0E0" stroke-width="1" filter="url(#shadow9)"/>
  <rect x="60" y="232" width="6" height="88" rx="3" fill="#42A5F5"/>
  <rect x="80" y="246" width="44" height="44" rx="22" fill="#42A5F5" fill-opacity="0.1"/>
  <text x="102" y="276" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="20" font-weight="bold" fill="#42A5F5" text-anchor="middle">2</text>
  <text x="144" y="270" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="17" font-weight="bold" fill="#212121">Use Aggressive Token Compression for Small Models</text>
  <text x="144" y="296" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#616161">Pixel shuffle at r=4 provides 16× token reduction with no accuracy loss for compact VLMs. This eases</text>
  <text x="144" y="314" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#616161">attention overhead and enables longer-context modeling within the same memory budget.</text>

  <!-- Takeaway 3 -->
  <rect x="60" y="334" width="1160" height="88" rx="10" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="#E0E0E0" stroke-width="1" filter="url(#shadow9)"/>
  <rect x="60" y="334" width="6" height="88" rx="3" fill="#0D47A1"/>
  <rect x="80" y="348" width="44" height="44" rx="22" fill="#0D47A1" fill-opacity="0.1"/>
  <text x="102" y="378" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="20" font-weight="bold" fill="#0D47A1" text-anchor="middle">3</text>
  <text x="144" y="372" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="17" font-weight="bold" fill="#212121">Extend Context Length via RoPE Scaling</text>
  <text x="144" y="398" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#616161">Scaling from 2K to 16K tokens (RoPE base 10K→273K) unlocks higher image resolution and multi-image</text>
  <text x="144" y="416" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#616161">understanding. Fine-tune on mixed long/short-context data for robust generalization.</text>

  <!-- Takeaway 4 -->
  <rect x="60" y="436" width="1160" height="88" rx="10" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="#E0E0E0" stroke-width="1" filter="url(#shadow9)"/>
  <rect x="60" y="436" width="6" height="88" rx="3" fill="#2E7D32"/>
  <rect x="80" y="450" width="44" height="44" rx="22" fill="#2E7D32" fill-opacity="0.1"/>
  <text x="102" y="480" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="20" font-weight="bold" fill="#2E7D32" text-anchor="middle">4</text>
  <text x="144" y="474" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="17" font-weight="bold" fill="#212121">Sub-1GB Inference Is Achievable</text>
  <text x="144" y="500" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#616161">SmolVLM-256M uses only 0.8 GB RAM and outperforms the 300× larger Idefics-80B. Enables deployment</text>
  <text x="144" y="518" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#616161">on smartphones and low-power edge devices with real-time throughput (~80 tok/s on Apple Silicon).</text>

  <!-- Takeaway 5 -->
  <rect x="60" y="538" width="1160" height="88" rx="10" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="#E0E0E0" stroke-width="1" filter="url(#shadow9)"/>
  <rect x="60" y="538" width="6" height="88" rx="3" fill="#FF8F00"/>
  <rect x="80" y="552" width="44" height="44" rx="22" fill="#FF8F00" fill-opacity="0.1"/>
  <text x="102" y="582" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="20" font-weight="bold" fill="#FF8F00" text-anchor="middle">5</text>
  <text x="144" y="576" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="17" font-weight="bold" fill="#212121">Fully Open-Source for Reproducibility</text>
  <text x="144" y="602" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#616161">All model weights, training data, code, and the HuggingSnap mobile app are released as open source.</text>
  <text x="144" y="620" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#616161">Promotes reproducibility and accelerates community research in on-device multimodal AI.</text>

  <!-- Implications callout -->
  <rect x="60" y="642" width="1160" height="34" rx="6" fill="#0D47A1" fill-opacity="0.08"/>
  <use data-icon="lightbulb" x="76" y="649" width="20" height="20" fill="#0D47A1"/>
  <text x="104" y="664" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#0D47A1">Implication:</text>
  <text x="200" y="664" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#0D47A1">Efficient architecture design — not scaling — is the path to democratizing multimodal AI on consumer hardware.</text>

  <!-- Footer -->
  <rect x="0" y="690" width="1280" height="30" fill="#F5F7FA"/>
  <text x="60" y="708" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="10" fill="#9E9E9E">SmolVLM: arxiv.org/abs/2504.05299 | Hugging Face & Stanford University, 2025</text>
  <text x="1220" y="708" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="10" fill="#9E9E9E" text-anchor="end">9 / 9</text>
</svg>

arguments.content:
# 01_cover

Welcome to this presentation on SmolVLM, a family of compact vision-language models developed by Hugging Face and Stanford University. SmolVLM demonstrates that architectural efficiency — not raw scale — is the key to deploying multimodal AI on consumer hardware.

[Pause]

Today we'll walk through three critical design decisions that enable sub-1GB inference: balanced compute allocation, aggressive token compression, and extended context lengths. We'll see benchmark results showing competitive performance against models 300 times larger.

Key points: (1) SmolVLM spans 256M to 2.2B parameters (2) Sub-1GB GPU RAM for smallest model (3) Fully open-source release
Duration: 1 minute

---

# 02_problem_motivation

[Transition] Let's begin by understanding why we need small multimodal models in the first place.

State-of-the-art vision-language models like Idefics-80B require enormous compute and memory resources. [Data] Molmo-A1B-7B, one of the best efficient open-source models, still demands 27.7 GB of GPU RAM — far beyond what any mobile device or edge system can provide.

[Pause]

Mobile and edge devices typically have less than 4 GB available for ML inference. Cloud-based solutions add latency, cost, and privacy concerns. The question is: can we achieve competitive accuracy at less than 1 GB RAM? SmolVLM answers yes — with 0.8 GB, the 256M model outperforms the 300 times larger Idefics-80B.

Key points: (1) Current VLMs require 27+ GB RAM (2) Edge devices limited to under 4 GB (3) SmolVLM achieves 35× RAM reduction
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 03_architecture_overview

[Transition] Now that we understand the motivation, let's examine how SmolVLM achieves this efficiency through its architecture.

SmolVLM uses a five-stage pipeline. First, input images are split into sub-images. These are encoded by a lightweight SigLIP vision encoder with only 93 million parameters. The encoded features pass through a pixel shuffle module that compresses visual tokens by 16×. A linear projection maps the compressed features into the language model's input space, where they are concatenated with text token embeddings and processed by SmolLM2.

[Pause]

Three critical architectural findings drive this design: balanced encoder-LM compute, extended context length, and aggressive token compression. We'll explore each in the next three slides.

Key points: (1) Current VLMs require 27+ GB RAM (2) Edge devices limited to under 4 GB (3) SmolVLM achieves 35× RAM reduction
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 03_architecture_overview

[Transition] Now that we understand the motivation, let's examine how SmolVLM achieves this efficiency through its architecture.

SmolVLM uses a five-stage pipeline. First, input images are split into sub-images. These are encoded by a lightweight SigLIP vision encoder with only 93 million parameters. The encoded features pass through a pixel shuffle module that compresses visual tokens by 16×. A linear projection maps the compressed features into the language model's input space, where they are concatenated with text token embeddings and processed by SmolLM2.

[Pause]

Three critical architectural findings drive this design: balanced encoder-LM compute, extended context length, and aggressive token compression. We'll explore each in the next three slides.

Key points: (1) Five-stage pipeline from image to language (2) 93M SigLIP encoder — not the larger 428M variant (3) Three key findings underpin the architecture
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 04_compute_allocation

[Transition] The first finding challenges a common assumption: that bigger vision encoders always help.

When paired with a 135M language model, the 93M SigLIP-B/16 encoder actually outperforms the 428M SigLIP-SO400M encoder. [Data] The smaller encoder achieves roughly 44% average benchmark score versus 38% for the larger one — a 4.6× parameter savings with better performance.

[Pause]

This pattern holds at the 360M LM scale as well, where both encoders perform similarly. Only at the 1.7B LM scale does the larger encoder begin to justify its 10% parameter overhead. The design principle is clear: match encoder capacity to language model capacity, and avoid over-investing in vision when the language model is the bottleneck.

Key points: (1) 93M encoder beats 428M encoder for small LMs (2) Encoder size only matters at 1.7B+ LM scale (3) Balance is more important than maximizing any single component
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 05_token_compression

[Transition] The second key innovation is aggressive token compression through pixel shuffle.

Pixel shuffle is a space-to-depth operation that rearranges spatial features into channel dimensions. [Data] At a shuffle factor of r=4, this reduces visual tokens by 16× — from 64 tokens in an 8×8 grid down to just 4 tokens, while preserving information in 16 additional channels.

[Pause]

Why is this so important for small models? Attention complexity scales quadratically with token count. By reducing tokens 16×, we dramatically cut attention overhead and enable longer-context modeling within the same memory budget. Larger models can afford r=2 with only 4× reduction, but compact VLMs benefit significantly from the more aggressive r=4 compression with no meaningful accuracy loss.

Key points: (1) r=4 pixel shuffle gives 16× token reduction (2) Quadratic attention savings from fewer tokens (3) No accuracy loss for compact models
Duration: 2.5 minutes

---

# 06_context_length_scaling

[Transition] The third finding involves extending the context window to handle more visual information.

Default transformer context is limited to 2K tokens, which means only one or two sub-images fit per input — severely limiting image resolution and multi-image understanding. SmolVLM extends context to 8K tokens for the smaller models and 16K for the 2.2B variant.

[Data] This 8× context increase was achieved by adjusting the RoPE positional encoding base from 10,000 to 273,000, combined with fine-tuning on mixed long and short-context data. The result: more sub-images per input means higher effective image resolution and better accuracy across all benchmarks.

Key points: (1) Context scaled from 2K to 16K tokens (2) RoPE base adjustment from 10K to 273K (3) Longer context enables higher resolution understanding
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 07_benchmark_performance

[Transition] Let's look at the numbers. How does SmolVLM actually perform across established benchmarks?

The team evaluated across 11 benchmarks spanning single-image understanding, multi-task reasoning, and video comprehension. [Data] SmolVLM-256M achieves a 44% average — at just 0.8 GB RAM. The 500M model reaches 51%, and the 2.2B model hits roughly 60% using 4.9 GB.

[Pause]

For context, Molmo-A1B-7B, the strongest efficient open-source baseline, requires 27.7 GB of RAM. SmolVLM-2.2B rivals its performance across most benchmarks while using less than one-fifth the memory. Perhaps most striking: SmolVLM-256M outperforms the 300 times larger Idefics-80B, a model released just 18 months earlier. Architectural efficiency has outpaced brute-force scaling.

Key points: (1) 44% / 51% / 59.8% average across three model sizes (2) 0.8GB to 4.9GB RAM vs 27.7GB for Molmo (3) 256M surpasses 300× larger Idefics-80B
Duration: 2.5 minutes

---

# 08_on_device_deployment

[Transition] These benchmark numbers translate directly to real-world deployment through HuggingSnap.

HuggingSnap is an open-source iOS app that runs SmolVLM entirely on-device — no cloud, no latency, complete data privacy. [Data] On a Pro M1 Max with 64 GB, the 256M model achieves approximately 80 tokens per second at batch size 1. Even on a consumer MacBook Air M3 with 16 GB, it delivers around 55 tokens per second.

[Pause]

The throughput scales roughly linearly with batch size. At batch 64, the 256M model reaches nearly 1,000 tokens per second on high-end Apple Silicon. This means real-time multimodal inference is practical on hardware millions of people already own — with zero cloud dependency and full offline capability.

Key points: (1) ~80 tok/s on M1 Max, ~55 tok/s on MacBook Air M3 (2) Linear batch scaling to ~1000 tok/s (3) Fully local, private, offline-capable
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 09_key_takeaways

[Transition] Let me close with five actionable design principles from SmolVLM.

First, balance encoder and language model compute — don't over-invest in vision. Second, use aggressive token compression for small models — pixel shuffle at r=4 costs nothing in accuracy but saves 16× in tokens. Third, extend context via RoPE scaling to unlock higher resolution. Fourth, sub-1GB inference is achievable — SmolVLM-256M proves it. And fifth, open-source everything to accelerate the field.

[Pause]

The broader implication is that efficient architecture design — not scaling — is the path to democratizing multimodal AI on consumer hardware. The code, weights, data, and mobile app are all publicly available for the community to build on.

Key points: (1) Five concrete design principles for efficient VLMs (2) Architecture efficiency beats scale (3) All artifacts are fully open-source
Duration: 2 minutes
